articleSnapshots.originalTitle: Sydney cockatoos reveal how animal culture helps them adapt to city life
articleSnapshots.fullContent:
by Santina Russo, University of Zurich

edited by Swati Mestri, reviewed by Robert Egan

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies. Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

Sulfur-crested cockatoos are surprisingly smart. In Australian cities such as Brisbane and Sydney, they've learned how to turn on drinking fountains by twisting the handle with their feet. In Sydney, they're even able to lift the lids of municipal garbage cans to get to the leftover food scraps inside.

However, when the birds do this, they scatter garbage and regularly create a real mess. That's why local residents have started securing their garbage cans: They place weights on the lids to weigh them down or use sticks to jam the hinges.

But the cockatoos, which can grow up to 50 centimeters (20 inches) tall, often manage to overcome even these new obstacles and open the garbage cans. They can pass on these skills to fellow members of their own flock and to neighboring cockatoo communities.

Although this battle of the garbage cans may be annoying for residents, it's very useful for researchers like Lucy Aplin, an evolutionary biologist at UZH: This scenario offers her the perfect place to start studying the social learning behavior of these birds.

Cockatoos belong to the parrot family, one of the most intelligent animal families on the planet. Parrots, for example, are able to learn new sounds throughout their lives, a skill that otherwise only whales, dolphins, crows and humans possess. This talent is one reason some parrot species are able to mimic human speech in a deceptively realistic way. Within the parrot family, sulfur-crested cockatoos are among the brightest.

But one thing's for sure: "Intelligence on its own is not enough for a new skill to spread within a species," Aplin says. Research already tells us that a certain degree of behavioral flexibility is also required—as well as a social network so information that has been gleaned is passed from one individual to the next and continues to exist for a long period of time, Aplin explains. In short, "It needs a culture."

In early summer 2026, the evolutionary biologist is in Sydney with her research team to study sulfur-crested cockatoos in the city. Among other things, the team is conducting experiments with the animals at the Royal Botanic Garden near the Sydney Opera House. From there, Aplin sends a video showing her latest experiment, featuring a cockatoo flying to an octagonal plexiglass container about half a meter (1.6 feet) in diameter.

The container consists of compartments that the bird has to open in different ways to get to the treat inside: an almond. The animal approaching the container is a male with a marking on his wing, number 11.

"We've named him Watermelon," Aplin writes in the video's commentary. Watermelon is one of the best-known cockatoos in the neighborhood because he's trusting and often visits balconies. Without hesitation, he pulls open a small drawer with his beak and grabs the almond inside.

Watermelon has never solved a task like this before. Aplin has come to appreciate that most cockatoos quickly understand how these drawers work. In the next task, Watermelon has to pull a lever to grab the almond. He swiftly accomplishes this, too.

The third puzzle seems a bit more difficult. The cockatoo has to twist the bottom of the compartment with his beak to free the almond. He fiddles around, and it takes him several attempts before he manages to do this as well. Then he flies off.

The researchers devise tests like this to study the birds' motor and cognitive skills, and their goal is to understand what needs to come together for the birds to solve problems using innovative behavior. The cockatoos are happy to play along, and not just because they love almonds.

They're naturally curious creatures and aren't afraid of people. What's more, the birds can recognize the researchers because they always wear the same blue coveralls and attract attention with a whistle. "The cockatoos now flock toward us as soon as we show up," Aplin recounts.

The evolutionary biologist has known many of the birds for years. Members of her team mark each animal with a pattern comprising three dabs of paint—using a small sponge and without having to catch the birds. This enables them to track which individuals interact with each other—which ones groom each other, which ones sleep or look for food together, and which animals visit neighboring groups of cockatoos.

During their lives, sulfur-crested cockatoos are estimated to interact with around a thousand members of the same species. "This means they have many more encounters than most primates," Aplin says.

The researchers record the birds' flight patterns using lightweight GPS transmitters that they attach to their legs. The transmitters drop off on their own after about a week. All these methods combine to provide insights into sulfur-crested cockatoos' behavior, cognitive abilities and extensive social networks.

Australian cities are particularly ideal places to study how animals adapt their behavior to urban areas, Aplin says. That's because they're young: Sydney has existed for only around 240 years. The cockatoo population in the Royal Botanic Garden still lives in the same trees, which are more than 300 years old, as it did in the 18th century.

Cockatoos live to be around 50 to 60 years old. This means that, unlike bird populations in Europe, these cockatoos have lived in an urban environment for only a few generations. The city expanded around them, and the clever birds learned to adapt.

One reason these birds have this ability is their comparatively large, well-connected brains. Cockatoo brains are similar in size to those of capuchin monkeys, which are three times heavier, and contain the same number of neurons as macaque brains, despite macaques being an even larger species of monkey.

"This brain allows the cockatoos to process information incredibly quickly," Aplin says. Along with their social network, this gives them the ability to develop new behaviors as a community.

They also demonstrate this capacity to adapt in their quest to conquer municipal garbage cans. In earlier studies, Aplin's team analyzed precisely how the cockatoos open these cans. To do this, the researchers once again needed help from local residents. Residents can use the Citizen Science app to report whenever cockatoos open garbage containers in their neighborhood.

"This gives us a picture of how the behavior is spreading," Aplin says.

In addition, the researchers used video recordings to analyze the technique the birds used to open the containers. It quickly became apparent that, even though the cockatoos are successful in their endeavor more often than residents would like, opening the garbage cans takes a great deal of effort. The birds first have to lift the lid with their beaks and feet, then hold it while scuttling forward along the rim before they can let the lid tip back.

"We've observed that, although significantly more birds try to open the garbage cans, more fail than succeed," Aplin says. Only around a quarter of the cockatoos that try actually manage to do it. Some successful birds take months to get really good at opening the garbage cans.

First, the task is physically demanding because garbage can lids are heavy. Second, the whole process presents a real cognitive challenge because it involves several steps. Aplin's analyses show that the biggest stumbling block for cockatoos is realizing that they can't lift the lid while they're still standing on it.

The researchers conducted another experiment to demonstrate how important social networks are to cockatoos' ability to adapt. They taught two individual birds that they could also eat bright red or blue almonds, then set up feeders containing these colorful almonds in their group. The researchers observed how rapidly things progressed: Within 10 days, even cockatoos living 10 kilometers (6 miles) away were willing to accept these colorful treats.

The team also obtained evidence that the cockatoos' appetite for the colorful almonds had spread through their social networks and that they'd learned from each other predominantly through imitation. "This shows how quickly niche behavior can spread through social learning," Aplin says. So it's no wonder that cockatoos are still very much in contention to win Sydney's battle over garbage.

Sulfur-crested cockatoos are not the only smart birds. We know from laboratory experiments that crows are able to solve complex puzzles and use tools in the process. For example, they've learned to drop nuts from high-rise buildings to crack them open. Or they throw nuts onto the road so they get squashed by cars.

However, one important aspect makes crows different from cockatoos: "They're much less curious," Aplin says. "Crows tend to avoid doing things they're not familiar with. Cockatoos, on the other hand, are attracted to new things and quickly engage with them." This makes them more innovative.

The inconspicuous great tits are also incredibly good at learning new things. In England in the 1920s, they managed to open the foil tops on milk bottles so they could nibble on the cream floating at the top. This was around 30 years before culturally learned behavior was first observed in monkeys. As a result, more and more tit populations throughout England began to steal cream.

Just like cockatoos, tits pass on new behaviors through their social networks, as Aplin's studies have shown. This snacking on cream continued until the type of milk bottle was replaced along with its cap—making the milk tit-proof once more.

articleSnapshots.fullContent: U.S. diesel prices broke another record last week, topping $6.50 per gallon. In Europe, fuel prices are soaring, and shortages are looming over already struggling economies. There is simply not enough refining capacity in the world to make up for the loss of Middle Eastern and Russian barrels. And there is no quick fix. Last week, Russia said it would extend a ban on diesel exports until the end of October, as Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries continued, despite President Donald Trump's call on the Zelensky government to stop attacking energy infrastructure, blaming the diesel price surge solely on those attacks. The latest attack came on Sunday, targeting one of Russia's largest refineries. However, the loss of fuel supply from the Middle East is much larger, the Wall Street Journal reported last week, citing figures from the International Energy Agency showing the amount of diesel output lost in the Middle East was three times as high as lost Russian supply. Now, there are calls in Congress for a U.S. ban on diesel exports. Rep. Tim Burchett tabled a bill to that effect last week, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune has backed the proposal. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum oppose it as a bad idea that would ultimately backfire, but the very fact that some legislators considered an export ban suggests the supply situation is pretty grim even for the world's largest oil producer. Related Hormuz Blockage Puts Qatar's $83 Billion LNG Bet at Risk Diesel prices underpin the price of pretty much everything else. When they rise, other prices follow, notably food prices, to which people are particularly sensitive. This is of particular concern in Washington ahead of the midterm elections in November, hence the idea of an export ban. A ban could bring down prices at home, but it would push prices even higher elsewhere, aggravating an already quite grave fuel supply crisis. It is a crisis that no one could have foreseen, but also one that might have arguably been less grave had there been more refining capacity in the world. The fact is that over the past decade or so, a lot of refineries have been shut down under pressure from the net-zero movement that has come to dominate energy policies, mainly in Europe, but also in the U.S. under Democratic administrations. Refining had become a losing game for many, so they either shut down or converted their capacity to biofuels. "We've seen the oil majors effectively reduce their exposure to that sector because the returns on actual capital employed have been poor," Wood Mackenzie senior VP for refining, chemicals, and oil markets Alan Gelder told the Wall Street Journal. "The classic phrase we used was 'How do you make a small fortune Take a large fortune and build a refinery.'" While refineries closed in Europe and the United States, however, Middle Eastern petrostates built new ones, coming to account for a bigger portion of global refining capacity. Profit, per the experts cited by the WSJ, was not the primary motivation. Employment and domestic fuel supply security were. Now, that capacity has been compromised and some of it has been damaged by Iranian strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure and there is no one to pick up the slack, with U.S. refiners already operating at rates as high as they can. To add insult to injury, there is one refinery in Europe sitting idle because it is the property of Russia's Lukoil, which the Trump administration sanctioned last November, prompting the company to put its international business up for sale. According to a recent report by the Financial Times, a deal between Lukoil and Carlyle Group for the latter's acquisition of the business had become "bogged down in an inter-agency process involving the National Security Council, State Department and Department of Energy," leaving urgently needed refining capacity offline. "There is significant underutilised refining capacity across Lukoil's European assets that could help bring additional refined-product supply to market and ease pressure on fuel prices," Carlyle said, as quoted by the FT, referring probably to the Romanian Petrotel refinery, which has been idled since the U.S. sanctions went into effect. Lukoil's Bulgarian facility is operating. Petrotel has a capacity of about 50,000 barrels daily. This is not a huge amount of fuel, but in the current crisis, every barrel matters. There is no solution to the world's fuel problem in sight. Tanker traffic via the Strait of Hormuz remains severely depressed, Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries continue, and if the U.S. bans diesel exports, according to the WSJ, China and India may follow its example, plunging the rest of the world into hitherto unseen levels of fuel shortages. The biggest loser of the situation, it appears, will be Europe, due to its heavy dependence on energy imports in both crude oil and refined products, and its shrinking refining capacity. By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

Changes could save £33bn and result in average of four extra years of good health for people, report says

The NHS in England could prevent 20,000 deaths and save £33bn a year by cutting red tape and boosting productivity, a report says.

Research by the Health Foundation found the health service has been held back for decades by excessive regulation, short-term planning and insufficient capability to deliver major change.
